topic: How a map finds the fastest route

opening.say: Picture a map as a bunch of dots, with roads connecting them, and every road has a number on it.
That number is how many minutes the road takes. A short road in traffic can cost more than a long empty one.
So the question becomes: out of all the ways to get from start to finish, which one adds up to the smallest total?

more.say: Say one way is three roads costing five, four, and six minutes. Add those up and that trip costs fifteen minutes.
Another way is just two roads, costing eight and nine. That's fewer turns, but seventeen minutes, so it's actually the slower trip.
Checking every possible trip would take forever on a real map, so the trick is to be smart about which dots you look at first.

plan.setup: Watch how the search spreads out from the start.
plan.narration: [[start-glows]]We begin at the start dot, with cost zero. [[neighbors-lit]]Then we look at its neighbors and write down what each costs. [[pick-cheapest]]Always grab the cheapest dot we haven't finished. [[update-costs]]From there, maybe we've found a quicker way to something. [[path-traced]]When we reach the finish, we trace back.
plan.plan:
start-glows: the start dot S lights up with a zero cost label, all other dots grey with infinity labels.
neighbors-lit: roads from S pulse, and the dots next to S get cost labels equal to the road minutes, for example four and seven.
pick-cheapest: the dot with the smallest label, four, turns solid, meaning its cost is final and cannot be beaten.
update-costs: from that dot, a road gives a neighbor a lower total than before, so its label changes from seven to six.
path-traced: the finish dot is reached and a bold line walks back along the cheapest roads to S, with total cost shown.
plan.close: Why is it safe to lock in the cheapest dot first?
